extract_html:
Antimony is a fascinating chemical element with the symbol Sb (from its Latin name, stibium) and atomic number 51. It is a shiny, silvery-grey metalloid, meaning it has properties of both metals and non-metals. In nature, it is most commonly found as a sulfide mineral called stibnite.

Antimony has a rich history across the world, but it holds a particularly special place in Indian culture and medicine. For thousands of years, stibnite has been known in India as Surma or Anjanam. It was ground into a fine powder to create traditional eye cosmetics (kohl), believed to protect and cool the eyes in the hot Indian climate. In ancient Indian medical systems like Ayurveda and Unani, specifically in the branch of Rasashastra, antimony is carefully processed to create traditional medicines.

Beyond ancient remedies, antimony played a starring role in modern Indian science. In 1920, the brilliant Indian physician Dr. Upendranath Brahmachari, working in Kolkata, synthesized an antimony compound called urea stibamine. This groundbreaking discovery became a highly effective cure for kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis), saving millions of lives and earning Dr. Brahmachari multiple Nobel Prize nominations!

Today, China is the world's leading producer of antimony, largely from the Xikuangshan Mine in Hunan. The metal is extracted by heating stibnite and mixing it with carbon or iron. In the modern world, antimony is an unsung hero hiding in everyday items. It is often mixed with lead and tin to make strong alloys used in bullets, solders, and engine bearings. It also strengthens the lead plates inside car batteries, acts as a powerful flame retardant in clothing and plastics, and is even used to make the tiny semiconductors that power our electronics.

sections.Characteristics: Antimony is a fascinating metalloid, meaning it shares properties with both metals and non-metals. When pure, it is a shiny, silvery-grey substance that is surprisingly brittle—so brittle that it can be easily crushed into a powder! It does not react with air or water at room temperature, making it quite stable, but it will catch fire if heated strongly, producing a thick white smoke.
sections.Isotopes: Like many elements, antimony comes in different forms called isotopes, which vary slightly in weight. In nature, you will find two stable, naturally occurring isotopes of antimony: 121Sb and 123Sb. Scientists have also created about 37 artificial, radioactive versions in laboratories, but these break down over time.
sections.Occurrence: Antimony is not very common—it ranks 63rd in abundance in the Earth's crust, making it as rare as silver! Although pure, native antimony is occasionally found in nature, it is almost always discovered locked inside a sulfide mineral called stibnite. Today, China is the largest miner and producer of this mineral, providing the lion's share of the world's antimony.
sections.History:
Antimony has an incredibly rich and ancient history, especially in places like India, Egypt, and the Middle East. As early as 3100 BC in predynastic Egypt, crushed stibnite was used as an eye cosmetic known as kohl.

In India, this same mineral has been known for millennia as Surma or Anjanam. Applied to the eyelids, Surma was a traditional staple believed to protect the eyes from the glaring sun and ward off infections. Ancient Indian medicinal practices, such as Ayurveda and Unani (specifically the alchemy-like branch called Rasashastra), carefully processed antimony into various therapeutic treatments.

Across the world, ancient scholars like Pliny the Elder and early Arabic alchemists wrote extensively about antimony's unique properties. In 1540, the Italian metallurgist Vannoccio Biringuccio published one of the first detailed guides on how to isolate pure antimony metal.

In modern times, antimony played a starring role in Indian medical history. In 1920, the renowned Indian physician Dr. Upendranath Brahmachari synthesized an antimony-based drug called urea stibamine. This was a miraculous cure for kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis), a deadly tropical disease. His discovery saved millions of lives globally and earned him multiple Nobel Prize nominations!
sections.Applications:
Today, antimony is an unsung hero of modern industry. Because it is so brittle on its own, it is almost always mixed (alloyed) with other metals like lead and tin to make them stronger and harder. These alloys are used to make bullets, durable solders, and plain bearings for machinery.

You can also find antimony hard at work inside car batteries (lead-acid batteries), where it helps stiffen the lead plates. Additionally, antimony compounds are heavily used to make flame-retardant materials for clothing, toys, and aircraft, keeping us safe from fires. Finally, highly purified antimony is used in tiny amounts to help create the semiconductors and microchips that power our electronic devices.
